description: Direct developer / local benthic mover. Brooded/direct developers with no pelagic larva; realized movement by crawling, burrowing, swimming or occasional vector-assisted transport.
Direct developer / algal resident rafter. Brooded/direct developers associated with macroalgae, vegetation or epifauna and able to raft with detached algae/plants.
Sessile epifauna with very short propagules. Sessile colonies or attached fauna with very short larval stage; realized spread can be extended by fragments or rafting.
Short pelagic / benthic-retained propagules. Short-lived larval or propagule phase, often with near-bottom retention and moderate passive dispersal.
Medium pelagic larval disperser. Typical meroplanktonic dispersers with weeks-long larval phase.
Long pelagic larval disperser. Long-lived planktonic larvae allow broad passive dispersal.
Very long pelagic larval disperser. Extended pelagic development producing very large dispersal potential.
Holoplanktonic / medusa drifter. Dispersal dominated by prolonged pelagic medusa/ephyra phase rather than a short benthic larva.
Host-mediated freshwater mussel. Freshwater mussels with fish-host transport during the larval stage.

Short-lived or sinking propagules that settle close to the parent. ALL ALGAE take M1 as the primary pathway, because spores are their primary dispersal unit; drifting thalli or fragments are recorded as a secondary pathway (M4 for durable leathery or calcified taxa, M5 for filamentous and soft ones). Also covers charophytes (oospores and bulbils), turion-forming plants, and seeds that sink within hours.
Angiosperm seeds and fruits that lack a pronounced floating adaptation.
Seeds and fruits with aerenchyma, air-filled pericarp or corky testa built for extended surface transport, and free-floating plants.
Fragments of thick, leathery perennial algae or robust vascular plants that resist breakdown and herbivory.
Floating fragments of soft, filamentous annual algae or sensitive vascular plants that decompose rapidly. The largest group.
